In the third session, we'll go into some advanced concepts in SQL.
For example, you can use some MySQL tools for organizing your code a little more.
A User Defined Function or a UDF is something you have available in MySQL.
You can use it to define functions for uses that aren't already readily available in MySQL through the standard SQL functions.
A stored procedure can be used to store code you find yourself running quite regularly with some changes here and there.
For example, let's say you have to run a given query daily for a daily report.
You can store this as a stored procedure and parameterize it so that it's also customizable, and every day when you run it, by varying a few inputs, you can make it answer the query that is most important to you that day while not having to write your code from scratch every day.
We'll also look at some tips and tricks for query optimization. In other words, tips and tricks that help you write more efficient queries that help you get to the answer of that business question more efficiently.
For any operation that requires you to search a big database, it helps to make an index in MySQL.
You will learn how many types of indexes you have available in SQL, and you will also learn how to make them and where to use them.
You'll also look at some best practices for coding that will help you further tune the readability and reusability of your code.
We will spend some time looking at the order in which the SQL compiler executes the different clauses of the SELECT statement.
Having this understanding will help us understand how the SQL compiler works, and it will help us tune our queries more to the point that they are very efficient, and the SQL compiler has a very easy job running them efficiently.
We'll close out by looking at joins vs. nested queries and comparing them for efficiency so we get a better sense of which one to prefer for what type of analysis.

USER DEFINED FUNCTIONS (UDFs) - INTRODUCTION What are UDFs? - Similar to UDFs in other programming languages, such as Python - MySQL UDFs do the following: - Accept parameter(s) - Perform action(s), such as a complex calculation - Return the result of the above action as a value Why use UDFs? - Ability to define functions not available directly in SQL - Improves code readability UDFs - EXAMPLE Syntax: /* Function Definition */ DELIMITER $$ CREATE FUNCTION function_name(func_parameter1, ) RETURNS datatype [characteristics] BEGIN <MySQL statements>; RETURN expression; END; $$ DELIMITER ; /* Function body must contain one RETURN statement */ Example: /* Function Definition */ DELIMITER $$ CREATE FUNCTION age_today(release_date date) RETURNS INT deterministic BEGIN RETURN year(current_date) - year(release_date); END; $$ DELIMITER ; /* Viewing Output */ SELECT mov_id, movie_title, age_today(movie_main.release_date) AS movie_age FROM movie_main;

395.text: UDFs has limited uses. So for example, it can only replace SQL functions or in other words, it can only be used in ways a built-in SQL function would have been used. For example, we've declared this function, age_today, and what it does is it calculates the age of a movie, it finds out how many years it has been since the movie was released. And we've used it in pretty much the same way we would have used a built-in SQL function such as CONCAT, or UPPER, or ABS, or something like that. But this is really the only use you can have out of a UDF. UDFs will not execute code blocks or code batches for you. They cannot be used to perform tasks such as updating age column here in the actual source table, or adding really this column to the source table. They'll only ever be used in querying the data, selecting something, and, and showing that to your screen. But if you recall, in Python, for example, you do have a lot of functions that don't necessarily return a set type of value but can just perform some actions and do a bunch of other things. And so that's where stored procedures come in. Stored procedures are this other type of stored routines in SQL that let you do all of these other things that a UDF cannot do. Perform actions, etc., and, and, and all of the other stuff that you would have wanted to execute. What is a stored procedure? So, essentially, it's just an object file in SQL that stores the code block that you want to keep running repeatedly. And so, essentially, just by saving a object file as a stored procedure, you can then run the code block within it with or without parameters repeatedly. For example, here we've used a stored procedure to output movies in the movie_main table that have age less than 20 years on the current date. So, to do that, we've defined this stored procedure, output_movies_with_age_less_than. And just like UDFs, the actual definition for this procedure, output_movies_with_age_less_than, should be written before you write the call statement. Also, just like for UDFs, you declare your delimiter change, and you will end with sort of resetting the delimiter to the semicolon, and between all of these, between these two keywords is where you'll write the procedure. You'll say, "Create Procedure", and then declare the procedure's name and say what input parameters you're going to be using, and then between the BEGIN and END keywords, you'll be writing the main body of your procedure.

397.text: Let's now look at some more differences between stored procedures and UDFs. So if you might recall, uh, UDFs are sort of very specific functions. They uh let in some parameter or some column and will give you as output something that can be used as a SQL column. So, they are similar to your existing SQL functions in usage such as UPPER, LOWER, CONCAT, and ABS. Uh and but that's the really the only functionality they are available for. A stored procedure is available to you for general purpose use. Uh the usage can be not just returning a column, for example, but updating it or doing something else, performing an action that doesn't neatly fit into sort of your standard SQL function format. Uh and so for that reason, stored procedures are able to uh not really ask you to return a value. They give you the option to either return it if that's something you want, or not really return it. Uh but for a UDF, it is mandatory to return something. Uh so you can use it in your SQL columns. Uh they are also different in how they are uh how they approach compiling and execution. A stored procedure is only compiled once uh and then it's just executed whenever it's called. Uh so it's a little efficient in sort of how it uses its runtime. Uh but user defined UDFs are actually compiled every time they are called or executed. A stored procedure can call a function within itself and a UDF is not really able to call a procedure. It can call a function but not really a procedure. Uh and again, a UDF can only use the SELECT clause, but with a stored procedure, you have sort of a variety of DDL or DML statements available, you SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, pretty much everything that uh you would usually use, you have available in in a stored procedure. Some more things you can do in stored procedures, for example, that you cannot do in UDFs is, you can use try-catch blocks to find out where the errors or exceptions are and then uh in advance sort of plan for them in stored procedures. You can use a CTE within your definition body in a stored procedure and not so much in a UDF. Uh and a stored procedure lets you define input or output parameters, uh but a UDF can only let you define input parameters.

398.text: So again, why indexing? As you might recall, we said that it helps for a table to have an index if you know that there is a column you're going to be looking up a lot and you sort of need that lookup to be efficient. When I say lookup, I mean something like, when I say I want to print all movies from the table movie_main where language is English. So I'm sort of just basically looking up in the column language for English language movies. So, again, we did say that indexing that column does make that lookup more efficient. Let's see why that is. So, for example, let's say I want to just output rows from this table that are English language movies. In this scenario, where this table is not sorted by the column language, but by some other column, I will have to do a lot of search operations. Basically, the compiler will have to compare for each row the value of language to English and check whether any of them match. And sort of this will have to be done for every single row in the table, from start to finish. But consider a scenario where the table itself is sorted by the language column. Here, if I ask for the same query to be run, I again just ask for all of the rows from this table where the language is English, it just has to keep searching until it finds a language different than English. So, for example, here the second I find a Hungarian language movie, I know that I have to stop because there cannot possibly be another English language movie after this. The table is sorted by language. So, yeah, I mean there's just no possibility of an English language movie existing in this table after after this row. So, what this essentially does is it it shortens the search space. As you can see, for the sorted table, you do have to perform fewer operations to be able to do the filtering that is needed.

399.text: So, a column like this is what we would call an index and this is essentially the strategy that is used by an index. We keep the entire table sorted by the column that is declared as the index and since it sort of makes lookups efficient, it is suggested that the index be the column that you find yourself searching over a lot, you find yourself using in a WHERE clause or looking up more often than the other ones. Here, for example, assuming that I will be using the language column a lot, assuming that I will be using a lot of WHERE conditions that involve the language column, I would say that maybe this column is the one that I should be using as an index, and and making making these these lookups more efficient for. You can also use an index for other columns as well. Obviously the table you can't guarantee will be sorted by both of these indexes, so the second one will be called a what I'm calling a secondary index. It does still make the lookup efficient for this column. We'll be looking later at how that happens, how it makes the lookup efficient, but the thing to note is that this is the secondary index, not really the main index. You can only have one index that you are extremely sure that the table is sorted by. The official names for these types of indexes are actually slightly different. They are called clustered and non-clustered indexes respectively. And it's if you look at the way the values sort of are grouped, you will see why they are called as such. So, for example, for the column language, you can see that sort of similar values are clustered together. English language movies are all clustered together. Japanese language movies are all clustered together, and so on. So, hence this is called a clustered index. We don't really see something like that for the movie_id column, so we call it the non-clustered index. Ideally, we would have seen this in ascending order, and so it would have been clustered in in in that sense. So that representation, the ascending order representation of this column is actually stored separately by SQL anyway. This is what SQL does for non-clustered indexes too to sort of make the lookup efficient. So, for example, here, let's say I want to find out and print all the movies from movie_main that have movie_id less than or equal to 215. It's clearly again efficient to look into this index and figure out which movies those are. This is again a much shorter search operation. And once you've done that, then SQL sort of uses an internal algorithm to map these rows in the index column to individual rows from your main main table and and provide them as the output. So, you just saw the different types of index data structures. Again, the ones that are sort of sorted and clustered together, those are called the clustered index types, and the other one is called the non-clustered index type. The clustered one you use for the column that you find yourself looking up most often. So that one, you can efficient, that one is the one you can optimize for efficiency. But in addition to index data structures, let's also look at the different types of indexes you have available. So, regardless of whether it's a clustered or a non-clustered index, your index can be a unique type which is, for example, in this table, the movie_id would be sort of a candidate for a unique type index. In general, for an internet-based database, things such as user_id sort of lend themselves very well to a unique type index column. The primary index is also often used. It's just the primary key of the table. If we feel that that is going to be sort of an import important column for analysis, then that is also something that can be used as an index. The regular index is sort of a column that isn't necessarily unique, but we do find ourselves searching it, looking it up a little regularly. So things such as the language here, for example, or a combination of columns sometimes language and country, those those are examples of regular indexes. A full-text index is very useful when you are looking up a column that has intensive text data. The movie_title column here, for example, The Amityville Horror, The Dark Knight, sort of these are long titles. And if you start writing complex conditions that are based on this column, then having a full-text index based on that column will really help. A descending type index is quite often useful when you want to look at recent data. So, for example, you can have a release_date descending type index for this table, and so essentially what that will do is it will sort of push all the latest releases to the top of the table. And so it becomes very, very, very efficient and very quick for SQL to look up a few rows of recent data. And lastly, this is the syntax you will be using to define indexes, add them, or drop them. Just keep in mind that these are DDL commands. When you're creating an index, you are just simply specifying you are going to be creating index with index name, on table_name, columns, etc. are the columns that comprise the index. So, this is sort of the way you will be creating the index. But the other operations that we have here, adding an index, or dropping an index from your table, these are all sort of DDL-level commands for the tables. So, you do start by specifying that you are altering a table and then, and then only, you sort of add keywords for what what action you are performing next.

400.text: Now look at the order in which SQL compilers execute different clauses of your query. Uh it is important to see and learn from it because this order is not exactly the same uh as the order in which uh you write your query. So uh it does help to learn this order, and to keep it in mind when you're writing your query, uh so you can write the best, the most efficient version of it, and get to sort of the answers of your queries uh quicker. For example, notice that the SELECT uh clause is all the way down here in the order, and the FROM and WHERE clauses are sort of at the top. What this means is that you can optimize uh the query as much as you want in the SELECT clause, you can have five columns instead of 20, but it's not nearly going to save you as much time as optimizing the FROM clause will, uh or the WHERE clause. So sort of figuring out which tables you want to query from and keeping that minimum, keeping your join simple and using the WHERE clause, really zeroing down on some rows only, the minimum number of rows you need to get to your answer, that's going to help your query run much faster than uh anything you you might change here in the SELECT part of the statement. Another classic example is the LIMIT clause, so in my sequel, for example, limit is sort of executed last, uh after everything, all the other clauses in your query are executed. And we often use LIMIT to sort of uh take the output we already have and limit it to the top 10 rows or 15 rows for example. Uh know that all my SQL is doing, its running is it's that it's running all the statements you've given it, and then once it's run all of it, then it's sort of just limits the the thing you see to 10 or 15 rows or however many rows you've given it. So in other words, sort of playing around with this number of limit rows is not really going to have almost any impact on how quickly your query runs and gets the result that you want. Uh it it will help to sort of optimize anything else, uh any any other part of your query, the limit part is not really helping you much in there.

So there are some best practices that are always suggested to keep your SQL code readable.
Following these will help other people quickly look at your code and figure out what's going on without you having to explain it a lot.
But more importantly, it will also help you sort of figure out what's going on.
Let's say a year down the line, or a few months down the line you look back at your own code, it might not be as obvious to you as it is right now as to what the code is doing.
But if you follow certain best practices and keep the code easy to read, it will be sort of easy for you to quickly ascertain that.

So the number one best practice is always to write appropriate comments.
The trick here is to not overdo it but write enough comments that you sort of get a general idea of what's going on.
If there's something that you feel needs to be called out so it's not that obvious and somebody would help from knowing it, it's always a good practice to sort of write that as a comment there.

You should also always use table aliases for SQL statements that involve more than one source.
So for example, let's say your query has a join and it's joining more than one table to get to that final table that it then selects from.
It always helps for each column to use table aliases, so it's easy to see which table each of those columns are coming from.
It also in general while writing the join itself helps you to have those aliases in case the tables have very big names.
We'll look at examples for a lot of these shortly, but that's the general idea for the second best practice here.

It also always helps to just assign very simple descriptive names for the columns and tables in your data set.
Don't make them very long and while they are short they should be able to convey swiftly and efficiently and correctly what the column is supposed to be or what the tables are supposed to be doing in your data set.

So the fourth one here is a big one. Any SQL keyword you ever use should be all in capital letters.
So for example, keywords such as FROM, WHERE, JOIN, SELECT. These should always be in capital letters and any names of columns, tables, or variables.
So for example, things like collisions, party age, movie main and gross et cetera, things like those in our examples, they should always be in lowercase.
Writing your query this way, keeping some parts of it in uppercase and some parts in lowercase will help you very very quickly, very visually figure out which part of your query is doing what and it does help you comprehend everything much quicker than if you weren't following these best practices.

It also helps if you maintain the right level of indentation for different sections of a query.
So what that means is let's say you have a complex query that involves a lot of SELECTs and FROMs and JOINs.
Indenting it the right way can sometimes go a long way in figuring out really quickly what is being selected from what table and what's being joined and we'll look at examples of that very shortly.

It also helps to use new lines for different sections of a query.
So if you are, for example, using multiple joins, then it helps to sort of have each of those in new lines and not in just the one same line just so that the code is a little more readable.

The last one is also a very important one.
So in your SELECT clause, let's say you have five columns, instead of writing all of them in one line and separating them by commas, it again helps to just write all of these column names in different lines.
So they are using up five lines and it's a little easier for you to figure out again what each of those columns is that you're trying to get from your source table.

A lot of these tips are best practices because SQL, unlike Python, will run even if you don't use the right indentation or the line breaks or everything, and even if you don't follow sort of the right cases.
SQL will still run the code without an error and give you the same answer, but it does help to be following all of these best practices so it's easier for you, again as stated earlier, to figure out what's going on in your code.
